claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys have superior structural and chemical stability at high temperatures compared with conventional low-entropy nanoalloys.
Configurational complexity significantly raises the energy barriers for atomic diffusion.
Higher diffusion barriers slow phase separation and grain-boundary migration.
The proposed initial material is a disordered, single-phase solid-solution nanoalloy containing multiple principal elements.
Grain boundaries and interfaces are the regions in which restricted atomic mobility preserves microstructural integrity.
High configurational entropy restricts atomic mobility in grain-boundary and interfacial regions.
Limiting atomic rearrangement suppresses phase separation.
Limiting atomic rearrangement suppresses grain growth.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will have lower grain-growth rates than conventional nanoalloys.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less phase decomposition than conventional nanoalloys.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, high-entropy nanoalloys will oxidize more slowly than conventional nanoalloys.
Conventional nanoalloys with fewer principal elements possess lower diffusion barriers.
Lower diffusion barriers cause conventional nanoalloys to undergo faster grain-boundary migration and phase separation at high temperatures.
The prediction is limited to temperatures near but below alloy melting points.
The prediction applies where thermally activated diffusion, rather than extreme oxidation or another chemical reaction, is the primary degradation mechanism.
A controlled comparison can use high- and low-entropy nanoalloys with similar average atomic sizes, exposed to the same temperature, atmosphere, and time intervals.
TEM, XRD, surface analysis, and tracer diffusion can measure grain growth, phase evolution, oxide thickness, and diffusion coefficients, respectively.
Failure to observe statistically significant reductions in grain growth, phase decomposition, or oxidation in the high-entropy samples would falsify the hypothesis.
